What Rami Ismail learned with his return to game development

What Rami Ismail learned with his return to game development
Indie dev advocate Rami Ismail has returned to making games after six years away from active development.
Bryant Francis
,
Senior Editor
,
GameDeveloper.com
November 3, 2026
schedule
7 Min Read
via Rami Ismail/Aesthetician Labs/Mystic forge
The video game industry wouldn't be the same without award-winning developer Rami Ismail. Even though the celebrated indie developer
parted ways with Vlambeer co-owner Jan Willem Nijman in 2020
and
sold his shares in the studio in 2024
, he's maintained his status as a globetrotting sword-for-hire helping small studios accelerate their work and pitching in on projects, particularly in developing or underrepresented regions. But he itch to jump back in and direct another game only grew stronger and stronger as the years went by. Now he's back and about to launch
Australia Did It:
End-of-the-World Railway Defense Business.
It's a turn-based strategy game (with a hell of a name to chew on), a very drastic shift from the fast-paced games like
Nuclear Throne
and
Luftrausers
that he and Willem Nijman used to collaborate on a decade ago. And returning to active development meant grappling with how much had changed. "It's a very different industry," he observed in an interview with Game Developer. "It is more brutal. It is far more risk averse than it has ever been."
Related:
Busting myths in game writing ft. Bruno Dias, Aysha Farah, & Andrea Saravia Perez
Ismail's return to active game development in this more "brutal" game industry comes as layoffs and closures have driven industry professionals to ask themselves a hard question: will they ever get to make another video game? He doesn't have the answer to that question—but his experience does illuminate what it's like for developers jumping back into the trenches, showing not only how to adapt to change, but also how their expertise still matters in this brave, uncertain new world.
Australia Did It
has an unusual origin story
Ismail had one major leg-up for venturing back into development. Unlike many of his peers rushing to event to event to pitch publishers and scrounge up funding, Ismail was lucky enough to be approached by publisher
Mystic Forge
, who pitched him on the idea of backing his next game.
"I don't think I've ever been pitched by a publisher to make a game," Ismail said, explaining that the company was motivated to support development in order to "stress test their processes and making sure they're all set up." He teamed up with Rochester, NY-based studio
Aesthetician Labs
and other collaborators like the artist "
castpixel
," musician
Max Caulkins
, and visual effects wizard
Jack Gutmann
, and embarked on a journey that ends next week with the game's launch with additional development support from
Dreams Uncorporated
.
But after launch, the
Australia Did It
team will shake hands and go their separate ways. This is one major way Ismail said he's adapting to the modern game development landscape. He and Willem Nijman always agreed that Vlambeer should never grow to be larger than two people, but now even that studio structure doesn't feel sustainable. "There's just no there's no variant of game development currently that offers stability," he said. The point of the studio model was that it was supposed to keep developers employed to build institutional knowledge and personalized best practices—but building a company means mitigating risk, and Ismail wanted to make a riskier, more unusual game.
Related:
Why it's still worth making immersive sims ft. Harvey Smith & Ben Horne
"I can't build a careful version of
Australia Did It
," he said. "This has to be a big swing... and the the only reasonable way to build this seemed to be to bring together a team [that wasn't obligated to always stay together]." And building a "risky" version of
Australia Did It
was especially important for Ismail, who lived through the saga of seeing his game
Ridiculous Fishing
cloned a decade before today's rush of indie game cloning. Making a game this unusual offered a "moat" that copycats would struggle to cross.
Ismail explained that the assembled development team had to quickly reckon with the fact that though everyone involved had good working relationships with each other, they didn't have those shared best practices that come with a studio model. "The first months was really about figuring out like what the game was and also [asking] 'how does this team communicate?' Who talks?' 'When do they talk?' 'What process do we use?'" He praised Aesthetician Labs' Sam Magnolia for leading the way in this effort, taking the role of game producer off of Ismail's shoulders. "As the person who has the creative director hat, I can't also have the producer hat, right," he said. "That's that's too much power consolidated into one voice."
Related:
Control Resonant director lays out case for avoiding excessive 'yellow paint'
Releasing that responsibility also supported Ismail's vision of taking a "big swing" with
Australia Did It
. A producer worried about timelines, stake, and scope can't also pitch the biggest, most far-out, and uncertain ideas. Ismail described it as a more "gig-like" experience, which follows a broader trend in modern developed economies of more and more knowledge-based jobs becoming freelance or short-term based, offering everyone the job stability of
a backup musician
.
He's not opposed to working with the
Australia Did It
development team again, or even one day returning to a more stable studio model. But the way he sees it, this is the best way to make the kinds of break-the-mold games that put him and Willem Nijman on the map at Vlambeer.
Learning the rules of a new genre
It's often assumed that developers moving from one studio to another will stick to their areas of expertise, often working in the same game genre. That's not been the case for Ismail.
